messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 19-year-old African American man in his first year working as a UX designer, living alone and trying to establish himself in a field he had once found exciting. He came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed into vigilance. When he describes what happened, he does not speak about a single dramatic assault so much as a sustained period in which ordinary routines became contaminated by fear. A person he had briefly interacted with online began sending him messages that quickly turned intrusive and possessive. At first the contact seemed merely uncomfortable, but it escalated into repeated texts from new numbers, comments that referred to where he had been that day, and appearances near places he regularly used. What unsettled him most was the way the stalker seemed to know his patterns before he had told anyone them directly. Walking out of his office one evening and seeing the same figure across the street, half-lit by a bus shelter ad, gave him the feeling that nowhere in his day was truly private anymore.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame began to make sense of the experience in ways that have remained fixed. He had come to believe that the world is fundamentally dangerous, not in an abstract way but in the specific sense that an ordinary day can turn threatening without warning. He speaks as though safety is a temporary illusion other people are naive enough to trust. From his perspective, danger announces itself only after it is already close. He says you never really know what can happen next, and for him this is not a figure of speech but a rule he now lives by. He scans people’s faces on the train, notices who is standing too long outside the building, checks whether a car has passed twice. At 19, he sounds older when he talks this way, as if the stalking taught him a lesson he did not want but now feels compelled to obey.

He also carries a persistent conviction that what happened reflects something about his own actions. He replays the early exchanges and the bits of personal information he shared, criticizing himself for having been too open, too polite, too visible online. In session, he circles back to small decisions—the tone of a reply, the choice not to block the first account immediately, posting from familiar locations—as if somewhere in those moments there must have been a point at which he failed to protect himself. He does not describe himself as reckless, but he clearly holds himself responsible for not anticipating malice sooner. Beneath that self-blame is the sense that if he had behaved differently, he might have preserved the version of life in which going to work, getting coffee, or taking a walk home did not require calculation.

His job has become one of the places where these beliefs are most visible. As a UX designer, he works in an open-plan office where people move between desks, meeting rooms, and common areas, and he finds it hard to relax in a space with glass walls and easy entry. He notices every unfamiliar person who pauses near reception. If he has to stay late to finish a prototype, he becomes acutely aware of the dimming floor, the reflection in the windows, the vulnerability of leaving the building after dark. He chooses his seat in meeting rooms based on sightlines to the door. Even when there is no clear sign of threat, he assumes he needs to stay especially careful. Coworkers have experienced him as distracted and guarded, though he has told very few of them why. Being single and relatively new to adult life had once felt full of possibility; now it seems to him like one more reason he has to watch out for himself because no one else necessarily will.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by the effort of living this way while still feeling unconvinced he could afford to stop. He did not come in saying he wanted to “feel better” so much as wanting to know whether it was possible to be less on guard without becoming foolish. What frightens him most is the idea that the fear may be the only thing keeping him safe, and that letting it down would mean inviting something worse. At the same time, he can see how much of his life is now organized around danger and regret. He is hoping, cautiously, for some way to move through the world without treating every ordinary moment as the start of another threat.
